summary: Gives guidelines to help authors of RTP payload format specifications make good design choices. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: This is a tip sheet for people who write the rules for packing audio and video into network packets.

why avoid ip fragmentation for rtp
subtitle: Advice for designing RTP payload formats so every packet that arrives is still useful when others are lost.

tldr.problem: Authors of RTP payload formats must pack codec output into packets, but the Internet can lose, duplicate and reorder packets, and a poorly chosen packetisation makes loss worse.
tldr.mechanism: The guidelines say a payload format should remain useful under moderate loss, align packets with codec frame boundaries, avoid relying on IP fragmentation, and carry a little decoder state where needed.
tldr.outcome: Following them yields formats that are robust on best-effort networks. The RFC is a Best Current Practice and has since been updated by RFC 8088.

today: RFC 2736 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 36) from December 1999 and has been updated by RFC 8088. Read the two together when writing a new payload format.

sections.title: Purpose of the Guidelines
sections.content:
This RFC gives general guidelines for authors of RTP payload format specifications, the documents that say how a particular kind of media data is packed into RTP packets. It tries to capture experience gained as RTP evolved.

The principles apply to almost all data types, but the examples are audio and video codecs. The document is a Best Current Practice.
sections.eli5: It is a tip sheet for people who decide how to pack sound and pictures into network packets.

sections.title: Application Level Framing
sections.content:
RTP was designed around Application Level Framing (ALF), described by Clark and Tennenhouse. The idea is that an application can cope with misordered or lost packets in many ways: ignore the loss, re-send the data, or send new data that supersedes it. That choice exists only if the transport handles data in Application Data Units (ADUs), each of which can be processed out of order. The ADU is the minimum unit of error recovery.

Each ADU must carry enough information to be processed immediately. In a video stream, the compressed data in an ADU must decompress even if earlier ADUs were not received, and it must say where it belongs in the image and which frame it came from. A packet is a natural ADU for many applications.

An RTP packet header already lets a packet be identified and decoded regardless of order or earlier loss, but only if the payload formats follow the same philosophy. The RFC adds that this implies smart, network-aware end-points that adapt to the limits of the network.
sections.eli5: Each puzzle piece should come with enough of a picture on it that you can place it even if other pieces never show up.

sections.title: Channel Characteristics
sections.content:
For best-effort transport of RTP over UDP/IP, the RFC lists four facts: packets may be lost, may be duplicated, may be reordered, and are fragmented if they exceed the MTU of the underlying network. Loss characteristics of a link can vary widely over short periods.

Relying on IP fragmentation is called a bad design strategy. It raises the effective loss rate and lowers goodput, since if one fragment is lost the remaining fragments, which already used bottleneck bandwidth, must be discarded. It also loads routers that fragment and end-systems that reassemble.

Transit time between two hosts is not constant, because of jitter from queueing behind cross-traffic and because of routing changes. A playout buffer can compensate for jitter, but routing changes are impossible to predict and hard to handle gracefully.
sections.eli5: The mail system can lose, copy or shuffle your postcards, and a big parcel gets chopped up, so if one chop is lost the whole parcel is wasted.

sections.title: The Core Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC states two requirements. First, the stream should still be useful in the presence of a moderate amount of packet loss. Second, ideally all the contents of every packet should be decodable and playable regardless of whether earlier packets were lost or arrived late.

For the first, payload formats should be designed for the public best-effort Internet, where moderate loss is normal. The RFC gives 5% loss as not uncommon, and notes that TCP steady-state models indicate a 5% loss rate with 1KByte packets and a 200ms round-trip time gives TCP about 180Kbit/s. A format that does not assume loss should say so up front, and is then a special purpose format unsuitable for the public Internet without special network support.

For the second, three rules follow. Packet boundaries should coincide with codec frame boundaries, so a packet holds one or more complete frames. A codec's minimum unit of data should never cross a packet boundary unless it is larger than the MTU. If a frame is larger than the MTU, the payload format must not rely on IP fragmentation and must define its own fragmentation mechanism, which can also allow packet-level forward error correction.
sections.eli5: Make every packet useful on its own, put whole pieces in each packet, and if a piece is too big, cut it in a way you planned, not however the network happens to.

sections.title: Frames, Fragmentation and Decoder State
sections.content:
The RFC works through codec examples. A codec frame is the minimum unit that has meaning to the codec. For PCM audio it is one byte, so packetisation does not matter. For GSM audio a frame is 20ms, and splitting one over two packets would make partial frames in neighbouring packets useless, so GSM is packetised with several whole frames per packet, typically four in current implementations.

For H.261 video, a frame unit is a Group of Blocks (GOB), one twelfth of a CIF video frame, and GOBs can be up to 3KBytes. The first H.261 payload format split large GOBs arbitrarily, which still forced the receiver to discard packets after a loss. The better approach adds a little extra information at the start of each packet so the stream can be split on macroblock boundaries, letting a smarter depacketiser rebuild a valid bitstream without discarding data that arrived.

Some codecs, such as LPC or GSM, need the decoder state to track the encoder state. Whole frames per packet may not be enough, because after a loss the decoder is out of step and the audio is distorted for a while. Sending all the state would defeat a low bit rate, so the RFC recommends that such formats should normally consider a small extra header carrying the most critical state, to reduce distortion after loss.
sections.eli5: Pack whole sentences into each postcard. If the reader needs to remember something from the last card to understand this one, write a short reminder at the top.

sections.title: Parameters, Header Extensions and Header Compression
sections.content:
Codec parameters, such as a choice between two Huffman tables, can be conveyed four ways: out-of-band signalling before the media, out-of-band signalling that can change mid-session, a change in the RTP payload type field, or including the parameter in the payload format. The last allows robust adaptation but is less efficient. Changing a parameter mid-session out of band is generally discouraged, because the change must be synchronised with the media stream.

Extra header information is best carried in the payload section. The RTP header extension should not be used for payload-specific information, since it wastes bandwidth, needs a new RTP profile or profile extension, and makes FEC schemes harder. It is only appropriate when the extension applies across a wide range of payload types.

Designers should also know about RTP header compression. It works best when the RTP timestamp increases by a constant value between packets, so formats that send packets out of order compress less well. Designers are encouraged to look for alternatives where possible.
sections.eli5: If the reader needs a special instruction, put it on the card itself where it travels with the message, rather than on a separate note that might be lost or arrive at the wrong time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Formats designed with these guidelines are robust under real network conditions. Formats designed for special purpose networks that assume negligible loss may compress slightly better, but are more fragile and so easier targets for denial-of-service attacks.

Designers should specify correct behaviour for anomalous conditions, such as illegal field values or mismatches between length fields and actual data. The correct action will normally be to discard the packet.

Payload encryption is covered by the RTP specification, but formats that spread an ADU over several packets, or depend on packets relating to several ADUs, may limit where the encryption key can safely change. Also, automatically adding FEC in response to loss can increase congestion and worsen the problem, which at worst could amount to a denial of service attack, so safeguards against abuse should be in place.
sections.eli5: Plan for odd or broken postcards, and do not answer lost mail by sending ten times more mail, because that clogs the post office.
